Timeshare Scam UK: How to Spot and Avoid Holiday Property Traps

Timeshare scams promise affordable holidays and investment returns—but deliver decades of unwanted contracts and mounting fees.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-07-02 · 7 min read

timeshare scam UKtimeshare fraudholiday property scamtimeshare exit scamfake timeshare investment
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Report it — call Action Fraud on 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland: 101), and forward scam texts to 7726.

What is a timeshare scam and how does it trap you?

A timeshare scam is a scheme where fraudsters or aggressive sales operations sell you a long-term contract to use a holiday property for a fixed week or weeks each year. The scam works because the initial pitch sounds attractive: you pay a one-time fee or deposit, then enjoy cheap holidays at resorts worldwide. In reality, you become locked into a contract lasting 10, 20, or even 40 years. Hidden costs emerge quickly—annual maintenance fees, property taxes, exchange fees, and insurance—often totalling hundreds of pounds yearly.

The property may be in poor condition, the promised exchange network may not work as advertised, or the resort may be in a location you never wanted. Scammers use high-pressure sales tactics, fake testimonials, and misleading comparisons to hotel costs to make the deal seem irresistible. Once you sign, exiting the contract is extremely difficult and expensive, leaving victims trapped paying fees for decades.

Red flags that signal a timeshare pitch is a scam

  • **Unsolicited contact offering a free holiday or prize.** Legitimate timeshare companies rarely cold-call or email with 'free' holiday offers; scammers use these to get you to a high-pressure sales event.
  • **Pressure to sign or pay a deposit immediately.** Genuine contracts allow time to read terms; scammers rush you to commit before you spot the trap.
  • **Vague or evasive answers about annual costs.** If the salesperson won't clearly state maintenance fees, property taxes, or exchange charges upfront, they are hiding the true cost.
  • **Claims that you can easily resell or exit the contract.** Timeshare resale is notoriously difficult; anyone promising a quick exit or buyback is lying.
  • **Promises of guaranteed rental income or investment returns.** Timeshare is not an investment; scammers falsely claim you can rent weeks to tourists and profit.
  • **The resort or property is in a remote or unfamiliar location.** Scammers often sell timeshares in overseas destinations where you cannot easily inspect the property or pursue legal action.
  • **Testimonials from 'happy owners' that sound scripted or generic.** Real reviews are specific and varied; fake ones are suspiciously uniform and enthusiastic.
  • **A salesperson who changes the terms or price mid-conversation.** This is a classic pressure tactic to confuse you and close the deal before you realise what you are signing.

How the scam unfolds: from first contact to being locked in

The scam typically begins with an unsolicited phone call, email, or text offering a free or heavily discounted holiday, a prize draw entry, or an exclusive investment opportunity. You are invited to a 'presentation' or 'seminar' at a resort or sales office, often in a holiday destination. Once there, you are seated with a salesperson in a high-pressure environment. They show glossy brochures, testimonials, and comparison charts claiming timeshare is cheaper than hotels. They emphasise the 'limited-time offer' and create urgency by suggesting the deal expires today.

You are offered a deposit or initial payment, sometimes framed as a 'booking fee' or 'membership fee', which is actually the start of your contract. The salesperson glosses over the fine print—annual maintenance fees, property taxes, and the length of the contract. Once you sign, you receive a contract that is often 20+ pages long, written in dense legal language, with key terms buried in clauses. By the time you realise the true cost and commitment, you are legally bound.

Cancellation rights exist in the UK (a 14-day cooling-off period), but scammers often make this period difficult to exercise by burying cancellation instructions or claiming fees apply.

How to verify if a timeshare offer is genuine

Before attending any timeshare presentation or signing anything, take these steps. First, search the company name online alongside 'scam', 'complaints', or 'reviews'—look for patterns of negative feedback on consumer forums and review sites. Check whether the company is registered with Companies House (companieshouse.gov.uk) and whether it has a UK address and phone number you can independently verify. Be extremely wary of companies based overseas or those that only provide email contact. Second, ask for the full contract in writing before the presentation, and read it carefully—legitimate companies will provide this without pressure.

Third, contact Citizens Advice or Action Fraud to check whether the company has been reported. Fourth, if the offer involves a property abroad, research the resort independently using Google Maps, recent photos, and independent reviews—do not rely on the company's own images. Finally, never pay any deposit or fee before you have read the entire contract, understood all annual costs, and had time to seek independent legal advice. If a salesperson refuses to provide these, walk away immediately.

What to do immediately if you have already signed a timeshare contract

If you have signed a timeshare contract, act quickly. First, check whether you are still within the 14-day cooling-off period (this runs from the date you signed). If you are, contact the company in writing immediately—send a letter by recorded delivery stating you wish to cancel and invoke your right to withdraw. Keep a copy. Second, do not pay any further fees or deposits while you are considering your position. Third, gather all documents: the signed contract, any emails, receipts, and promotional materials. Fourth, contact Citizens Advice (0808 223 1133) for free guidance on your rights and next steps.

Fifth, if you believe you were misled or the contract was sold under duress, report it to Action Fraud (0300 123 2040) and provide them with all evidence. Sixth, consider seeking legal advice from a solicitor who specialises in consumer law—some offer free initial consultations. Do not contact timeshare 'exit companies' that promise to get you out of your contract for a fee; these are often scams themselves and will take your money without delivering results.

Reporting a timeshare scam in the UK

Report timeshare scams through multiple channels to maximise the chance of action. Start by calling Action Fraud on 0300 123 2040 or reporting online at actionfraud.police.uk—provide all details of the company, the salesperson, the location of the presentation, and copies of any contracts or promotional materials. If you received unsolicited contact by email, forward it to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk. If you were contacted by phone or text, forward any SMS to 7726 (this alerts your mobile provider and the NCSC).

Contact Citizens Advice (0808 223 1133) to report the company and seek guidance on your consumer rights. If the timeshare is overseas, also report to the consumer protection authority in that country if possible. Finally, if you have lost money, ask your bank whether you can dispute the transaction or claim a chargeback—this is especially important if you paid by credit card, as you may have additional protection under Section 75 of the Consumer Credit Act. Keep detailed records of all reports and correspondence.

Frequently asked questions

Can I cancel a timeshare contract after the 14-day cooling-off period?

Cancellation becomes much harder after 14 days, but it is not impossible. You may have grounds to cancel if you can prove the contract was sold under duress, through misrepresentation, or in breach of consumer law. Contact a solicitor specialising in timeshare disputes or Citizens Advice for advice on your specific situation. Do not pay timeshare exit companies unless you have verified they are legitimate and have checked independent reviews.

I paid a deposit to a timeshare company and now I am worried it was a scam. What should I do?

Stop all further payments immediately. Check whether you are still within the 14-day cooling-off period and, if so, cancel in writing by recorded delivery. Report the company to Action Fraud (0300 123 2040) and contact your bank to ask whether you can dispute or reverse the payment, especially if you paid by credit card. Contact Citizens Advice (0808 223 1133) for free guidance on your rights and next steps.

Is it true that timeshare companies can force me to keep paying maintenance fees forever?

Timeshare contracts are legally binding and can last decades, but they are not truly 'forever'—they have an end date, which may be 20, 30, or 40 years away. However, you remain liable for annual maintenance fees, property taxes, and other charges until the contract ends or you successfully exit it. This is why timeshare is so profitable for scammers: victims are trapped paying hundreds of pounds yearly for decades. If you are in a contract, seek legal advice on your options to exit.

What is the difference between a legitimate timeshare and a timeshare scam?

Legitimate timeshare companies are transparent about all costs upfront, allow time to read contracts before signing, do not use high-pressure sales tactics, and provide clear cancellation procedures. Scams use unsolicited contact, pressure you to sign quickly, hide annual costs, make false promises about resale or rental income, and make cancellation deliberately difficult. If a timeshare offer feels rushed or the salesperson avoids answering questions about costs, it is almost certainly a scam.
